reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: One of the perforating dermatoses, characterised by umbilicated papules and nodules with a central keratotic plug through which altered collagen is extruded (transepidermal elimination)
Lesions are often intensely itchy and show the Koebner phenomenon, appearing in linear arrays along scratch marks
The acquired adult form is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, particularly in patients on dialysis
A rare inherited childhood form exists, precipitated by superficial trauma or cold
Commonly affects the extensor limbs, trunk, and backs of the hands, with lesions typically resolving over weeks to leave scars or hyperpigmentation as new crops appear
Diagnosis is confirmed on biopsy showing a cup-shaped epidermal depression with elimination of degenerate, basophilic collagen bundles through the epidermis
Pruritus and scratching are central to pathogenesis, so lesions cluster where the patient can reach
Management addresses the underlying disease and the itch, using emollients, topical corticosteroids, keratolytics, antihistamines, phototherapy, and control of pruritus
reference.pathophysiology: Reactive perforating collagenosis is a disorder of transepidermal elimination in which altered dermal collagen is extruded through the epidermis. Superficial trauma and, in acquired cases, the metabolic disturbances of diabetes and renal failure are thought to damage dermal collagen and provoke an epidermal response that channels the degenerate collagen to the surface. Persistent scratching in response to itch perpetuates the trauma and drives the characteristic Koebnerised, umbilicated papules, so that lesions cluster at accessible, frequently scratched sites and continue to recur while itch and the underlying systemic disturbance persist.
additionalDifferentials: Other perforating dermatoses (elastosis perforans serpiginosa, perforating folliculitis, Kyrle disease)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing a cup-shaped epidermal invagination with transepidermal elimination of collagen
Special stains (such as Masson trichrome and elastic stains) to characterise the eliminated material and distinguish it from elastic-fibre perforating disease
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to screen for diabetes mellitus
Renal function tests (urea, creatinine, eGFR) to detect chronic kidney disease
Assessment of dialysis status and adequacy in renal patients
Screening for other causes of pruritus (for example liver and thyroid function) where relevant
redFlags: Newly diagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes or chronic kidney disease uncovered by the skin findings
Intractable pruritus with a marked impact on quality of life and sleep
Secondary infection of excoriated, ulcerated lesions
Atypical or rapidly growing nodules requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy
reference.prognosis: The acquired form runs a chronic, relapsing course tied to control of the underlying systemic disease; individual lesions heal, often with scarring, but new crops recur while itch and metabolic disturbance persist.
pitfalls: Overlooking undiagnosed diabetes or renal disease in an adult presenting with perforating papules
Treating the skin without addressing the underlying itch and metabolic cause
Confusing it with prurigo nodularis or the other perforating dermatoses without biopsy
Underestimating the role of scratching in perpetuating lesions
